entries.d: in good times and bad times; whatever happens
x: My sister has supported me [[through thick and thin]].
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.d: to make a great effort to help or please someone
x: Our neighbours [[bent over backwards for]] us when our flat was flooded.
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.d: to make more effort than is expected of you
x: A real friend will [[go the extra mile]] when you really need help.
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.d: a friend who is only there when things are going well
x: When I lost my job, I quickly found out who was [[a fair-weather friend]].
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.d: said when you are happy to help a friend, meaning that helping is what friendship is about
x: “Thanks so much for helping me move.” “Don't mention it. [[What are friends for?]]”
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.t: You scratch my back and I'll scratch yours.
entries.d: if you help me, I will help you in return
x: Their partnership works on a simple principle: [[you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours]].
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.d: to fail to appreciate someone properly
x: Why did the friend stop doing favours? Because everyone kept [[taking him for granted]].
entries.s: Idioms & Expressions

entries.t: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
entries.d: a friend who helps you when you are in trouble is a true friend
x: He lent me his car when mine broke down: [[a friend in need is a friend indeed]].
entries.s: Proverbs

entries.d: family relationships are stronger and more important than other relationships
x: We argue a lot, but [[blood is thicker than water]]: I'd always help my brother.
entries.s: Proverbs

entries.d: you should take care of your own family before helping other people
x: Before you volunteer to help everyone else, remember that [[charity begins at home]].
entries.s: Proverbs

entries.d: clear limits between people help them get along well (Robert Frost)
x: We agreed who looks after the hedge, and we've never argued since: [[good fences make good neighbors]].
entries.s: Quotations

entries.d: nobody can live completely alone; everyone needs other people (John Donne)
x: Even very independent people need support: [[no man is an island]].
entries.s: Quotations

entries.t: The only way to have a friend is to be one.
entries.d: if you want friends, you have to be a good friend yourself (Ralph Waldo Emerson)
x: If you want people to call you, call them first: [[the only way to have a friend is to be one]].
entries.s: Quotations

entries.d: a request that is difficult to agree to because it asks a lot
x: Lending larger sums repeatedly is [[a big ask]], particularly if they have a history of not paying people back.
entries.s: Should you always lend money to family?

entries.d: in my opinion; from my point of view
x: [[From where I stand]], family loyalty does not mean you should put yourself in financial difficulty.
[[From where I stand]], support should strengthen people rather than make them permanently reliant on us.
entries.s: Should you always lend money to family?

entries.d: despite what has just been said; however
x: [[That said]], refusing to help someone you care about can make you feel guilty.
entries.s: Should you always lend money to family?

entries.d: feeling that you owe someone something because they helped you
x: Refusing to help can make you feel guilty or even [[indebted]] if they have supported you in the past.
entries.s: Should you always lend money to family?

entries.d: for the same reason; in the same way
x: [[By the same token]], having helped you once does not give them permanent entitlement to your money.
entries.s: Should you always lend money to family?

entries.d: the feeling or belief that you have a right to something
x: Having helped you once does not give them permanent [[entitlement]] to your money.
entries.s: Should you always lend money to family?

entries.d: too involved in someone's private life, in an unwelcome way
x: Families often give advice because they care, but helpful advice can quickly become [[intrusive]].
entries.s: How much advice should families give each other?

entries.t: I can see where they're coming from
entries.d: I understand their reasons or point of view, even if I don't fully agree
x: [[I can see where they're coming from]]: they may genuinely believe that experience gives them useful insight.
entries.s: How much advice should families give each other?

entries.d: despite that
x: [[Even so]], constantly telling another adult what they should do can undermine their autonomy.
entries.s: How much advice should families give each other?

entries.d: the freedom to make your own decisions
x: Constantly telling another adult what they should do can undermine their [[autonomy]].
entries.s: How much advice should families give each other?

entries.d: a very small difference between two things
x: There is [[a fine line between]] giving advice and trying to control someone.
entries.s: How much advice should families give each other?

entries.d: used to add an idea that goes further, often the opposite of what might be expected
x: [[If anything]], repeatedly offering unwanted advice may make the other person less likely to listen.
[[If anything]], constantly rescuing someone may prevent them from taking responsibility for their own situation.
entries.s: How much advice should families give each other?

entries.t: there's only so much you can do
entries.d: your ability to help or act is limited
x: [[There's only so much you can do]] before supporting someone begins to affect your own life.
entries.s: Should you drop everything for a friend in trouble?

entries.d: to stop what you are doing immediately in order to help someone
x: Being a good friend does not necessarily mean you have to [[drop everything]] whenever they need you.
entries.s: Should you drop everything for a friend in trouble?

entries.d: speaking for myself; as far as I am concerned
x: [[For my part]], I think the seriousness of the situation matters.
entries.s: Should you drop everything for a friend in trouble?

entries.t: that doesn't sit well with me
entries.d: I am not comfortable with that; it does not seem right to me
x: [[That doesn't sit well with me]], especially if the friendship becomes completely one-sided.
entries.s: Should you drop everything for a friend in trouble?

entries.d: to try to do more than you are able to, so that it becomes too much for you
x: Supporting somebody should not require you to [[overextend yourself]] indefinitely.
entries.s: Should you drop everything for a friend in trouble?

entries.d: willing to help and to adapt to what other people need
x: At first, you might try to be [[accommodating]], particularly if they are going through a difficult time.
entries.s: When do relatives start taking liberties?

entries.d: to behave too freely, without respecting someone's rights or kindness
x: If they invite people over without asking, they may be [[taking liberties]].
entries.s: When do relatives start taking liberties?

entries.d: used to introduce a point that is fair to the other side of the argument
x: [[To be fair]], family members often feel less formal with one another than ordinary guests do.
entries.s: When do relatives start taking liberties?

entries.d: despite what has just been said
x: [[That being said]], being family does not remove the need for basic consideration.
entries.s: When do relatives start taking liberties?

entries.t: you have to draw the line somewhere
entries.d: there is a limit to what you can accept
x: [[You have to draw the line somewhere]], especially when someone else's comfort comes at the expense of your own.
entries.s: When do relatives start taking liberties?

entries.t: when all is said and done
entries.d: when everything has been considered; in the end
x: [[When all is said and done]], family relationships are rarely based on a simple calculation of who owes what to whom.
There will always be exceptional circumstances, but [[when all is said and done]], caring about someone does not require sacrificing every boundary of your own.
entries.s: Do we owe our parents something in return?

entries.d: feeling that you owe someone something because they have helped you
x: Some people genuinely want to help their parents, while others may feel [[beholden to]] them.
entries.s: Do we owe our parents something in return?

entries.d: I would have doubts about; I am not completely convinced by
x: [[I'd have reservations about]] the idea that children automatically owe their parents unlimited support.
entries.s: Do we owe our parents something in return?

entries.d: used to give a reason that should be remembered or taken into account
x: [[After all]], raising a child is a responsibility parents choose to take on.
entries.s: Do we owe our parents something in return?

entries.d: used to introduce a point that contrasts with what has just been said
x: [[At the same time]], refusing to help a parent who is genuinely struggling may feel deeply uncomfortable.
entries.s: Do we owe our parents something in return?

entries.d: something that does not concern you, so you should not get involved
x: Should you say something, or is it [[none of your business]]?
entries.s: Should you get involved in a friend's relationship?

entries.t: that's not quite how I see it
entries.d: a polite way of saying that you disagree
x: [[That's not quite how I see it]] when people say friends should never interfere.
entries.s: Should you get involved in a friend's relationship?

entries.d: used to add a point that slightly changes or limits what you have just said
x: [[Mind you]], there is a difference between expressing concern once and repeatedly trying to make decisions for them.
entries.s: Should you get involved in a friend's relationship?

entries.d: too controlling; always trying to tell other people what to do
x: Becoming [[overbearing]] can damage the friendship and make the person defensive.
entries.s: Should you get involved in a friend's relationship?

entries.d: in the present situation; as things are now
x: [[As things stand]], adults ultimately have to make their own relationship decisions.
entries.s: Should you get involved in a friend's relationship?

entries.d: it applies to both sides; it has advantages and disadvantages
x: Should they automatically agree to help you move this weekend? [[It cuts both ways]].
entries.s: Should friends always return favours?

entries.d: the practice of exchanging help or favours so that both sides benefit
x: Friendship involves [[reciprocity]], but that does not mean every favour has to be repaid immediately.
entries.s: Should friends always return favours?

entries.d: used when you have just had a new thought or realised something
x: [[Come to think of it]], some friends contribute emotionally while others are more helpful in practical ways.
entries.s: Should friends always return favours?

entries.d: after thinking about all the facts
x: [[All things considered]], what matters is whether both people generally feel valued.
entries.s: Should friends always return favours?

entries.d: to accept or agree to something, often without really wanting to
x: You may initially [[acquiesce]] simply to avoid an argument.
entries.s: Is saying no to family selfish?

entries.d: used to introduce a different point that makes the previous one less certain
x: [[But then again]], constantly agreeing to things you do not want to do can create resentment.
entries.s: Is saying no to family selfish?

entries.d: despite the fact that
x: [[For all that]] family relationships involve obligation, protecting your own time does not automatically make you selfish.
entries.s: Is saying no to family selfish?

entries.d: you do not have to; nobody can force you to
x: [[You're under no obligation to]] agree to every request.
entries.s: Is saying no to family selfish?

entries.d: it is much more difficult to do than to talk about
x: [[That's easier said than done]], particularly when the person is close to us.
entries.s: How do you know when you've done enough?

entries.d: used to accept that something is reasonable, often before adding a reservation
x: [[Fair enough]], there will always be exceptional circumstances.
entries.s: How do you know when you've done enough?

speaking.q: “Blood is thicker than water.” Do you agree?
“Good fences make good neighbors.” Is that true for neighbours, friends and family?
“A friend in need is a friend indeed.” Who has been that kind of friend for you?
“No man is an island.” Can anyone really live without other people?
Should you always lend money to family?
How much advice should families give each other?
Should you drop everything for a friend in trouble?
When do relatives start taking liberties?
Do we owe our parents something in return?
Should you get involved in a friend's relationship?
Is saying no to family selfish?
How do you know when you've done enough?
